concept.name: Memory Allocators

relationships.description: Connects Memory Allocators to jvm internals and garbage collection in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: User-space memory allocators like jemalloc, tcmalloc, and mimalloc sit between your application and the OS kernel, carving large mmap/brk regions into thread-local size classes so malloc() and free() complete in ~15–30 ns without global lock contention or virtual memory fragmentation.
spark.keyTakeaway: Default glibc ptmalloc2 optimizes for general-purpose compatibility, not high-concurrency tail latency; switching to jemalloc or tcmalloc and tuning dirty-page decay routinely cuts RSS by 15–35% and eliminates multi-core lock stalls.

concept.whyItMatters: Every `malloc`, `new`, `Vec::push`, or string allocation in C, C++, Rust, Python, or JNI-heavy JVM services hits the user-space allocator before it ever touches the kernel. Under high thread counts or mixed object sizes, a poorly matched allocator causes severe internal/external fragmentation, multi-millisecond `mmap`/`munmap` TLB shootdowns, and RSS bloat that triggers Linux OOM-killer even when live heap usage is under 50%.
whenToUse: High-concurrency multi-threaded services (C++, Rust, Go cgo, or JVM with RocksDB/Netty off-heap buffers) experiencing futex contention inside `ptmalloc2` arenas.
Long-running caches and databases (Redis, MySQL, ClickHouse) with mixed allocation sizes (64 B to 1 MB) where external fragmentation steadily inflates RSS over days.
Latency-sensitive workloads where 99.9th percentile pauses must stay under 100 microseconds without sudden kernel `brk`/`mmap` or Transparent Huge Page (THP) compaction stalls.
whenNotToUse: Short-lived CLI tools or batch scripts that exit within seconds, where allocator warm-up and per-CPU cache metadata add unnecessary startup overhead.
Strictly bounded, fixed-size real-time embedded systems where dynamic allocation is banned and static slab pools or stack buffers guarantee deterministic O(1) memory.
Garbage-collected runtimes using pure managed heaps (pure Go or pure JVM without off-heap JNI) where the runtime's own bump-pointer allocator already bypasses `libc` malloc.
keyPoints: Allocators partition memory into segregated size classes (e.g., 8 B, 16 B, 32 B, ..., up to 32 KB) to bound internal fragmentation under ~12.5% while eliminating free-list search scans.
Thread-local caches (`tcache` in jemalloc/ptmalloc2) and per-CPU caches (using Linux `rseq` in tcmalloc) serve 95%+ of allocations lock-free in ~10–25 ns.
Cross-thread deallocation (Producer Thread A allocates, Consumer Thread B frees) bypasses thread-local fast paths and requires atomic remote-free lists or arena locking.
Returning freed pages to the OS via `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` drops physical RSS immediately but forces costly minor page faults on reuse; `dirty_decay_ms` balances RSS vs CPU.
Linux Transparent Huge Pages (2 MB THP) reduce TLB misses for large contiguous arrays, but can amplify small-page allocator fragmentation by 512x if `MADV_DONTNEED` only punches 4 KB holes.

examples.title: Redis RSS Bloat Under High Eviction Churn
examples.scenario: A 64 GB Redis cluster handling 200k writes/sec with mixed 100 B–16 KB keys saw RSS climb to 61 GB while `used_memory` stayed at 38 GB (fragmentation ratio 1.60), triggering OOM alerts.
examples.outcome: Compiling with `jemalloc` and enabling `activedefrag yes` alongside `dirty_decay_ms:1000` consolidated sparse 4 KB runs and purged dirty pages, dropping fragmentation ratio to 1.08 and reclaiming 19 GB of RAM.

examples.title: JVM + RocksDB Off-Heap Arena Explosion
examples.scenario: A Kafka Streams service running on a 64-core container with `glibc ptmalloc2` spawned 128 worker threads; RocksDB's C++ allocations created 512 arenas (`8 * cores`), driving native RSS 40% above the cgroup limit.
examples.outcome: Preloading `libjemalloc.so` via `LD_PRELOAD` with `MALLOC_CONF="narenas:16,dirty_decay_ms:2000"` capped arena proliferation, cut native RSS by 28%, and removed p99 latency spikes during compaction.

tradeOffs.factor: Thread-local cache size vs. Memory footprint
tradeOffs.pro: Larger `tcache` or per-CPU caches keep more size classes hot in L1/L2, eliminating cross-core synchronization and keeping allocation latency under 20 ns.
tradeOffs.con: With 200+ threads, each holding 2–4 MB of cached free blocks, idle thread caches can pin 500 MB–1 GB of unreachable RSS.

tradeOffs.factor: Aggressive OS page return (`dirty_decay_ms`) vs. Page fault CPU
tradeOffs.pro: Short decay windows (0–500 ms) invoke `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` quickly, keeping container RSS tightly aligned with live heap so Kubernetes doesn't OOM-kill.
tradeOffs.con: Immediately unbacking pages forces the kernel to zero-fill and fault in 4 KB pages on the next allocation burst, burning 5–12% extra system CPU.

tradeOffs.pro: Restartable sequences (`rseq`) bind caches to physical CPU cores rather than OS threads, capping cache overhead even when an app spawns thousands of goroutines or pthreads.
tradeOffs.con: Requires Linux kernel >= 4.18 for `rseq` and can suffer cache thrashing if the OS scheduler rapidly migrates a thread across NUMA nodes.

failureModes.name: ptmalloc2 Arena Proliferation
failureModes.description: In glibc, threads hitting contention spawn new 64 MB arenas up to `8 * CPU_COUNT`. In containers with 64 host cores but a 4 GB cgroup limit, native virtual and resident memory explodes.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4` for glibc workloads or switch to `jemalloc` with explicit `narenas` tuned to `2 * cgroup_cpus`.

failureModes.name: Producer-Consumer Remote Free Skew
failureModes.description: When I/O threads allocate request buffers and worker threads free them, the worker's `tcache` overflows while the I/O thread's cache starves, forcing constant slow-path arena mutex acquisitions.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `mimalloc` (which shards free lists per page with lock-free atomic remote-free lists) or batch-return buffers to an explicit object pool on the allocating thread.

failureModes.name: THP Compaction & Page-Zeroing Stalls
failureModes.description: Kernel `khugepaged` or synchronous THP allocation attempts to coalesce 512 contiguous 4 KB pages under memory pressure, stalling `malloc()` for 10–150 ms.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` to `madvise` (never `always`) and configure `jemalloc` with `thp:never` or `metadata_thp:auto`.

failureModes.name: False Sharing on Adjacent Small Allocations
failureModes.description: Two threads allocate separate 16-byte structs that land on the same 64-byte CPU cache line; frequent writes cause MESI cache-line bouncing across cores (~50 ns/write).
failureModes.mitigation: Pad hot per-thread structs to 64 bytes (`alignas(64)`) or use size classes >= 64 bytes for contended atomic counters.

commonMistakes: Assuming `free()` immediately returns RAM to the OS and diagnosing retained RSS in `top` or Prometheus as a memory leak.
Running `LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so` on static binaries (like Go or musl-linked Rust) where `libc` malloc symbols are not dynamically resolved.
Leaving `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` unset on high-core Kubernetes nodes running small-memory JVM/Python containers with native C extensions.
Benchmarking allocator throughput on a single thread, which completely hides lock contention, false sharing, and cross-thread free-list overhead.
Ignoring `mallopt(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD)` or `dirty_decay_ms` when workload patterns shift from steady-state caching to spiky multi-megabyte batch allocations.

sections.content:
## The idea

Calling the OS kernel (`brk` or `mmap`) on every allocation is far too slow: a syscall context switch plus page-table setup and zero-fill takes 500–2,000 ns, whereas modern services allocate millions of small objects per second. A user-space memory allocator acts as an amortizing cache over the kernel's virtual memory subsystem.

Instead of asking the kernel for 24 bytes, the allocator requests large aligned chunks (typically 2 MB or 4 MB extents/arenas) via `mmap` and subdivides them into fixed **size classes** (e.g., 8, 16, 32, 48, 64, ..., 14 KB). Each thread (in `jemalloc`/`ptmalloc2`) or physical CPU core (in `tcmalloc`) maintains a lock-free local cache of recently freed blocks for each size class. As long as the local cache has a slot, `malloc()` and `free()` execute in 10–30 ns with zero syscalls and zero cross-core synchronization.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a Rust HTTP server running `jemalloc` on 16 cores handling a 128-byte JSON header allocation followed by a 256 KB response buffer:

1. **Fast-path small allocation (128 B):** The worker thread maps 128 B to size class index 8. It pops a pointer directly from its thread-local `tcache` bin in ~12 ns. No mutexes, no atomics, no syscalls.
2. **Cache miss refill:** If the `tcache` bin for 128 B is empty, `jemalloc` locks only the specific arena bin (sharded across 16 arenas, so contention is minimal), pulls a batch of 32 blocks (4 KB slab) from the arena's active run, and refills `tcache`.
3. **Large allocation (256 KB):** Objects exceeding `tcache_max` (default 32 KB) bypass `tcache` entirely and allocate directly from the arena's extent tree (or `mmap` if no free 256 KB contiguous run exists), avoiding polluting small-object caches.
4. **Deallocation & Decay:** When the 256 KB buffer is freed, `jemalloc` marks those 64 pages as dirty. Rather than calling `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` immediately, it holds them for `dirty_decay_ms` (default 10,000 ms). If another 256 KB request arrives within 10 seconds, it reuses the already-faulted physical pages with zero kernel overhead; otherwise, a background/epoch purge returns the physical frames to Linux.

data.title: User-Space Allocator Fast Path, Arena Refill, and OS Decay

edges.label: 1. Pop size class
edges.title: Fast-path allocation
edges.description: Thread maps requested bytes to a size class and pops a block from its local cache without locking.

edges.label: 2. Batch refill
edges.title: Cache miss slab fetch
edges.description: When the local bin is empty, the allocator acquires the sharded arena bin lock and pulls a batch of blocks.

edges.label: 3. mmap extent
edges.title: Kernel page backing
edges.description: If no free extent satisfies the size, the arena requests a 2 MB chunk from the OS via mmap.

edges.label: 4. Push free block
edges.title: Local deallocation
edges.description: Small freed objects return to the freeing thread's tcache; cross-thread frees go to remote atomic lists.

edges.label: 5. Flush overflow
edges.title: High-watermark flush
edges.description: When a tcache bin exceeds its item limit, half the blocks flush back to the arena's dirty run list.

edges.label: 6. madvise purge
edges.title: Dirty decay return
edges.description: After dirty_decay_ms elapses, the allocator issues madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) to release physical RSS.

data.caption: Fast-path allocations stay inside the thread/CPU cache; only bin refills and decayed dirty pages cross into arenas or the OS kernel.

sections.content:
## How modern allocators differ

While all modern allocators use size classes and local caching, their concurrency and metadata models diverge sharply:

- **glibc `ptmalloc2`:** Uses a `tcache` (up to 7 items per bin) backed by up to `8 * cores` arenas. Free blocks store intrusive pointers inside freed user memory, which is fast but prone to heap-metadata corruption bugs and severe arena RSS bloat on high-core hosts.
- **`jemalloc` (Meta / Rust / FreeBSD):** Uses out-of-band bitmaps in slab headers, strict `dirty_decay_ms` / `muzzy_decay_ms` smoothing, and built-in heap profiling (`prof:true`, `jeprof`) that lets engineers capture live allocation flamegraphs in production with <2% overhead.
- **`tcmalloc` (Google):** Replaces per-thread caches with per-CPU caches using Linux `rseq` (restartable sequences), bounding cache RAM by core count rather than thread count—ideal for servers with 10,000+ threads.
- **`mimalloc` (Microsoft):** Shards free lists per 64 KB page and splits local vs. thread-delayed free lists using lock-free atomic CAS, excelling at asymmetric producer-consumer workloads.

## Allocator comparison

| Allocator | Local Cache Model | Cross-Thread Free | OS Page Return | Production Profiling |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **glibc ptmalloc2** | Per-thread `tcache` (7/bin) | Arena mutex lock | `MADV_DONTNEED` on top trim | `malloc_stats()` / `mallinfo2()` |
| **jemalloc 5.x** | Per-thread `tcache` (<=32 KB) | Arena bin lock + epoch merge | Time-based `dirty_decay_ms` | Built-in `jeprof` sampling |
| **tcmalloc (Google)** | Per-CPU (`rseq` on Linux >=4.18) | Lock-free transfer cache | Background page heap release | Built-in heap profiler (`pprof`) |
| **mimalloc 2.x** | Per-page sharded free lists | Lock-free atomic delayed list | `mimalloc` eager/timed reset | `mi_stats_print()` |

## Failure modes

**1. Silent OOM from fragmentation, not leaks:** An application holds 2 GB of live objects, but a single surviving 64-byte object in each 4 KB page pins 4 GB of dirty pages in RSS. Watch `jemalloc`'s `stats.active` vs `stats.allocated` (ratio > 1.25 signals fragmentation).

**2. `MADV_FREE` vs `MADV_DONTNEED` accounting illusions:** `MADV_FREE` marks pages lazily reclaimable without zeroing RSS immediately, causing Kubernetes cgroup `memory.current` and `top` to still count them until kernel memory pressure hits. For strict container limits, prefer `MADV_DONTNEED`.

**3. `fork()` deadlock:** Forking a multi-threaded process while another thread holds an arena mutex deadlocks the child process unless the allocator registers `pthread_atfork` handlers—always use `posix_spawn()` or `execve()` immediately after `fork()`.

## Production tuning and observability

You can diagnose allocator health in production without restarting services by inspecting process maps and allocator stats:

- **Check active vs. resident:** Compare `jemalloc` `allocated` (bytes requested by app), `active` (bytes in pages containing live data), and `resident` (physical RSS). A high `resident - active` gap means `dirty_decay_ms` is too long; a high `active - allocated` gap means external fragmentation from mixed lifetimes.
- **Tuned `MALLOC_CONF` baseline for containers:** `MALLOC_CONF="background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:2000,muzzy_decay_ms:0,narenas:8"` offloads page purging to background threads so request threads never stall on `madvise`.
- **Verify `rseq` for tcmalloc:** Check `grep rseq /proc/self/status` or kernel version (>= 4.18); without `rseq`, modern `tcmalloc` falls back to slower mutex-protected per-thread caches.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify whether your runtime uses `glibc ptmalloc2` (via `ldd ./binary`) and benchmark `jemalloc` or `tcmalloc` under realistic multi-threaded churn.
- [ ] Set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4` if staying on `glibc` inside memory-constrained containers on high-core hosts.
- [ ] Enable `background_thread:true` and tune `dirty_decay_ms` (1000–5000 ms) in `jemalloc` to bound RSS without causing page-fault CPU spikes.
- [ ] Disable system-wide `always` Transparent Huge Pages (`echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled`) to prevent 2 MB fragmentation amplification.
- [ ] Alert on `(rss_bytes - heap_allocated_bytes) / rss_bytes > 0.30` and capture `jeprof` / `pprof` allocation flamegraphs before blaming application code for a leak.

interviewProblems.title: Memory Allocators
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Memory Allocators. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: User-space memory allocators like jemalloc, tcmalloc, and mimalloc sit between your application and the OS kernel, carving large mmap/brk regions into thread-local size classes so malloc() and free() complete in ~15–30 ns without global lock contention or virtual memory fragmentation.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Sharded Arena & Slabs applies the primary invariant and coordinates with OS Virtual Memory.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, OS Virtual Memory experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4` for glibc workloads or switch to `jemalloc` with explicit `narenas` tuned to `2 * cgroup_cpus`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Default glibc ptmalloc2 optimizes for general-purpose compatibility, not high-concurrency tail latency; switching to jemalloc or tcmalloc and tuning dirty-page decay routinely cuts RSS by 15–35% and eliminates multi-core lock stalls.
Avoid trap: Assuming `free()` immediately returns RAM to the OS and diagnosing retained RSS in `top` or Prometheus as a memory leak.
Avoid trap: Running `LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so` on static binaries (like Go or musl-linked Rust) where `libc` malloc symbols are not dynamically resolved.
When to reach for it: High-concurrency multi-threaded services (C++, Rust, Go cgo, or JVM with RocksDB/Netty off-heap buffers) experiencing futex contention inside `ptmalloc2` arenas.
When to reach for it: Long-running caches and databases (Redis, MySQL, ClickHouse) with mixed allocation sizes (64 B to 1 MB) where external fragmentation steadily inflates RSS over days.

putItTogether.title: Putting Memory Allocators Together
putItTogether.summary: Default glibc ptmalloc2 optimizes for general-purpose compatibility, not high-concurrency tail latency; switching to jemalloc or tcmalloc and tuning dirty-page decay routinely cuts RSS by 15–35% and eliminates multi-core lock stalls.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Memory Allocators before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Compiling with `jemalloc` and enabling `activedefrag yes` alongside `dirty_decay_ms:1000` consolidated sparse 4 KB runs and purged dirty pages, dropping fragmentation ratio to 1.08 and reclaiming 19 GB of RAM.
